lines.text: Both batteries were off. Then the telegraph answered back.
September, eighteen fifty-nine. A tap in Boston makes a click in Portland, Maine. That's how news gets down the wire.
Then the sounder starts hammering by itself. Across town, the other lines go wild.
The signal cuts out. Then the current slams back! The operator jumps, and his chair shoots backward.
Across the network, sparks leap from the equipment. At one station, paper catches fire.
Boston looks down at the battery. What if they cut it off?
Cut it off? How do you expect me to hear you?
Portland puts down the lead. He waits.
Then comes the whole signal, every tap clear enough to read.
They send another test. Both leads are still on the desks. The current comes and goes, but when it steadies, they get right back to work.
A storm from the Sun shook Earth's magnetic field.
That change created an electric field at ground level. It pushed current through the long, grounded telegraph line.
The same storm lit up the sky with auroras.
They'd turned off their batteries. The Sun was still on the line.
